translation: ...another [mixture] distinct from the moist and cold one, and a third in addition to these, the dry and cold, distinct from the one that is at once dry and hot. Some of them, however, say that there exists a certain mixture that is moist and cold at once, and another hot and dry at once, but not the moist-and-hot nor the cold-and-dry; for it is not possible, they say, either for moisture to concur with a prevailing heat or for dryness with cold. For the moisture is consumed by the heat when it is in control, and thus the body becomes hot and dry at once; whereas it remains unconcocted and unworked-up in those bodies in which the heat is weak; so that it is necessary, when heat prevails, that dryness follow, and when cold predominates, that moisture attend it. These men, then, on these grounds have persuaded themselves that all the [mixtures] are two in number...

Aristotle, and likewise Theophrastus too, have stated precisely what one must look to in supposing a nature to be well-mixed or ill-mixed; but these men do not even know this, and when they hear them saying that the animal is moist and hot, or that the mixture of the child is moist and hot, they neither understand how these things are said, and they foolishly transfer the account to the seasons, as though it were the same thing, and not differing by a wide margin, whether one's own mixture is moist and hot or that of the air surrounding us. For it is not the same thing, nor is the mixture of an animal said to be moist and hot in the same way as the mixture of air is said to be moist and hot. What the cause of all these things was I shall now relate, and I shall show clearly to those willing to apply their minds how small errors among the...

...left-handed, nothing absurd. So too, then, a dog is moist and at the same time dry, and hot and at the same time cold, but not in relation to the same thing: for in relation to a man it is dry, but moist in relation to an ant, and in relation to a man hot, but cold in relation to a lion. And indeed it is hot insofar as it is living (for if something has died, it is not hot), but not hot in relation to another dog, if it should so happen. All these things, then, are said relative to one another by comparison; but those said as within the genus of animals are said in another way, as again also according to the species of animal. For a dog in relation to an ant and a bee is moist, but within the genus of animals dry; and of dogs themselves according to species this one is dry, that one moist, and another...

...the condition of nature that is best is judged by its activities. For indeed we say that any plant or animal whatever is best disposed at the time when it functions most finely: the excellence of a fig tree is to bring to maturity the best and most figs, and in the same way that of the vine is to bear in abundance the most and finest grapes, that of a horse is to run most swiftly, and of a dog to be utterly spirited for hunting and guarding but most gentle toward its own household. All these things, then, I mean both the animals and the plants, we shall say have the best and intermediate mixture within their own genus, not simply when there is an exact equality of the opposites, but when the proportion of that [mixture] according to capacity obtains. And we say that justice too is something of this kind: not what is equal by weight and measure, but by what is fitting...

...for if he were asking of what mixture it is, as among animals, one must make the answer itself with a view to the mean of all animals in mixture; but if simply and as in relation to all substance, then in that case one must already compare the opposites within it against one another, and consider them no longer by referring the mixture to the activities but to the bulks of the elements. But if he asked by comparing it in a determinate way to some particular thing, one must compare it to that alone; and still more if we were asked about one of the individual substances, as for instance Dion or this particular dog, what sort of mixture it has, one must not answer simply; for from this there arises no small opportunity for the sophists to quibble. For if you were to say that Dion is of a hot and dry mixture, it is very easy for him, taking up one of those drier and hotter than he, the...

...both those of animals and those of plants and those of all inanimate things, such as bronze and iron and stones and timbers, are ranked in the interval between those first [extremes]; for none of them is extremely hot or extremely cold or extremely moist or extremely dry, but either it is exactly in the middle of the opposites, so as to be no more hot than cold or dry than moist, or it has moved toward one of the extremes, so as to be more hot than cold or more moist than dry. If indeed it should be exactly in the middle in respect of each of the two oppositions, so as to be no more hot than cold or dry than moist, this will be called well-mixed simply; but when one has prevailed, either in the one antithesis or in both, it is no longer well-mixed. If indeed...

...the other antithesis: the soft nerve is no longer intermediate between hot and cold, but it falls short of heat by as much as it does of blood. So too all the other parts mentioned before are colder than skin by as much as they are more bloodless; and the very coats of the most blood-filled vessels, I mean of the artery and the vein, are bloodless and cold by nature, but by their proximity to the blood they are warmed and arrive at an intermediate state of mixture. The blood in turn itself has its warmth from the heart; for by nature that viscus is of all the parts of the animal at once the most blood-filled and the hottest, and next after it the liver. But the heart falls a little short of skin in hardness, the liver a great deal; and so it is moister than skin by as much as it is softer. And indeed also...

...and in the movements of the limbs; he is always of good colour and breathes well, and is intermediate between the sleepy and the sleepless, between the bare of hair and the shaggy, between the dark in complexion and the fair; and he has hair, when a child, rather more reddish than dark, but in his prime the reverse. Since we have also made mention of the difference in him according to the ages, it would be no worse now to say something about these as well. I wished, then, first to go through the causes of each of the signs mentioned; but since the inquiry into the ages is more pressing for the present matters and renders us best furnished for the discovery of the causes, we shall now take this up. Let us conceive, then, the animal just now being moulded in the wombs of those who bear it, so that we may recognise how it is most moist and most hot. For its first constitution is from...

...the nurses mould the limbs of infants as though they were of wax, so great is the moisture in the whole body of young children. But also if you should wish either to eat or to cut open and examine a young sacrificial animal, you will find the flesh mucous and flabby, and the whole bony kind resembling cheese that is just now curdling, so that the bodies of newborn animals are not even pleasant to eat on account of their excessive moisture; and this has happened most of all to the flesh of pigs and sheep, because they too are, above all, moister, whereas goats' flesh, because it is drier, is both better and more pleasant to eat. Conversely to the young sacrificial animals, those grown old have all their bones and all their ligaments quite dry and sapless and juiceless, and their flesh sinewy and hard, and their arteries and...

...a quantity of saliva collects in the mouth; but they also cough and spit up phlegm, showing thereby that the lung too is full of such a humour; and their stomach is filled with phlegm, and each of the joints is somewhat mucous. But none of these things stands against the bodies of those growing old being dry; for you will find the nerves and the arteries and the veins and the membranes and the coats of all the organs much drier than before, but plastered round them within and without either some phlegmatic humour or a mucous moisture. But so far are all such signs from showing old age to be moist that they seem to me even to bear witness to its dryness; for it is on this very account that each of the parts becomes drier, that it is no longer nourished as before, and now, through weakness of the heat, a quantity...

...it seems to me, now that the type of their arguments has been clearly recognised from what we have said; for both parties reason from afar and almost from secondary things to the prior, and they make their argument as though their hearers already knew how growth, how digestion, how nutrition comes about; and likewise they discourse on sensation and motion and the practical and natural activities, and they make mention of the generation of sleep and of the nature of foods, none of which is simply and easily knowable, but requires a very great deal of inquiry, and perhaps cannot even be discovered unless one first knew how to recognise a moist and dry and hot and cold mixture. For whatever of those things they say as though already knowing it, if someone compelled them to demonstrate it, they will of necessity require the account of mixtures that is now before us; so that through one another and...

...the argument before us must not take its proofs for them from things not yet known, but, as is both right and just, what is to be taken for the demonstration ought to be either one of the self-evident things or one of the things demonstrated beforehand. So one must make mention neither of the generation of sleep nor of digestion nor of growth nor of any other such thing, but let the inquiry proceed from the sole and bare substance of the underlying matters, just as we have also done through the first book. For having distinguished that what is in actuality is one thing and what is in potentiality another, we said that the account must first be made concerning what is already hot and cold and dry and moist in actuality, and then thus arrive at the things in potentiality. Now ready to hand for all and familiar is the [discrimination] of things already hot in actuality...

...positing principles and elements, to have strayed so far from the men who posited these as not to know that the principles of every demonstration are the things evident to sense-perception and to thought, and that whoever is in doubt about these inquires in vain about the rest, having left himself no starting point from which to begin. Whence, then, they turned to so long a wandering and undertook to seek by reasoning the discrimination of perceptible things, I for my part cannot even conceive; and for this reason I judge by touch what is hot in actuality, while if something is not yet hot but is fitted to become so, which indeed is also called hot in potentiality, this I try to discover by reasoning. But for them, I know not how, everything has been overturned, and a long rhetoric has been practised about arguments. These men, then, let us leave, having reminded ourselves of at least this much now too, that...

...nor is it reasonable at all to confirm the prior from the posterior. Let us judge, then, by sense-perception the hot and cold body, that at least which is already such in actuality and no longer in potentiality, setting aside the first judgement and all the other signs. And you indeed, as one who will judge well, I release to the test; my own judgement I shall myself expound. For touching many bodies in succession with care, not of children only or of infants but also of youths and of those in their prime, I found that neither party was speaking the truth, neither those who said the man in his prime was simply hotter nor those who said he was colder than the child. For if, removing all the other alterations from without, you were to examine the differences arising from age alone, neither appears to you simply hotter; for their heats differ in quality, owing to the unequal transpiration, through which also...

...spinal [marrow] by kind, but all the other marrows are of another nature. The brain is moister and hotter than the spinal marrow, and for this reason also softer; and moreover of the brain itself the front parts are moister by as much as they are also softer. Yet all these are not only moister than skin but also colder; and in general everything bloodless is colder than what is blood-filled. Nearest to skin is also the nature of the soft nerves, while that of the hard ones is just like the skin itself in respect of moisture, clearly, and dryness; for in heat it falls short by as much as it is reasonable for the wholly bloodless to fall short of a blood-filled body. The flesh of the spleen and that of the kidneys and that of the liver is moister than skin by as much as it is softer, and hotter by as much as it has more blood. And indeed the flesh of the heart too...

...catarrhs and coughs and runnings of the nose and a quantity of saliva; for all these show him to be colder and moister, and still more if upon chance occasions he falls into such conditions. Baldness, on the other hand, follows upon dryness, and the growth of dark and abundant hair is a sign of a good mixture of the brain. In this way, then, one must always inquire about mixture by examining each part separately, and not dare to pronounce about all from one, as some have done, saying that the snub-nosed are moist and the hook-nosed dry, and those whose eyes are small dry, and those whose eyes are large moist. This indeed is even disputed among them; for some, having assumed that the eyes are among the moist parts, in those in whom they find them larger [infer] a moistness of mixture in...

...the same thing, either to evacuate some moisture scattered about in certain regions, or to render the proper mixture drier. For a certain uneven ill-mixture arises in inflamed parts, the homoeomerous bodies not yet having departed from their proper nature but still being changed and altered, while all the regions between them are filled with the flux. All things, then, which are hot and moist in mixture, when applied to those in this state, evacuate that excess which has occupied the regions between the homoeomerous bodies, but are so far from drying the bodies themselves that they even contribute moisture to them. The truth, then, stands thus; but what has been said requires a demonstration, which, judging it to be too long to be appended in the present treatise, and moreover to require a hearer who understands about the capacity of drugs, I defer at least...

...if you will, the yellow bile, and that all the rest are hot incidentally through partaking of these: will it not be necessary that the animal become hotter in two ways, either by acquiring more hot humours or by having them hotter than before? To me indeed it seems quite so; and in the same way, I think, it will also become colder in two ways, either by the cold humours, such as phlegm and black bile, being bred in greater quantity, or by the quality alone being altered while the proportion of them all remains. What wonder, then, that so long as the food cold by nature, such as purslane and lettuce, is being digested, the body is filled with a cold quality, but when they have been digested thoroughly and have become good blood, the body becomes in turn hotter than itself by the generation of the hot humour? And indeed...

...the condition, if it is simple and one; but the judgement is determined by time in the following manner: what is manifestly seen to cool or to heat at the very moment of being applied would surely be such both in itself and through itself, whereas what does so in time might perhaps be brought to this by some incidental circumstance, just as in a case of tetanus in the middle of summer, for a young man of good flesh, an affusion of much cold water produces a recall of warmth. But that cold water does not heat in itself is clear from the first impact; for it produces a sensation of chilling, and indeed it chills the skin so long as it is being poured on it, and the warmth it furnishes neither in all bodies nor during the pouring, but only in young men of good flesh in the middle of summer, after the pourers have ceased. Just as, then, for those upon whom there falls...

...of the ease and the benefit, this is of necessity cold, if ever on other [bodies] it appears hot; for it will be found, when examined carefully, not to heat those in itself but by some incidental circumstance. Now when we say 'in itself' or 'primarily' or 'through none of the intermediates', the same thing is signified in effect by all these expressions; and the exercise of all these together with their proper examples we shall carry out in the treatises on drugs. Now, however, having recalled again what I have already said before, I shall try to put upon the present discourse its fitting end. For since the hot body was spoken of in many ways (for it is both that which has the extreme quality, the element itself, and that which is so named by predominance of that quality, and further that which is said in relation to another, either to the well-proportioned member of the same kind or to anything whatever...

...and with rose cerate it helps greatly, against which indeed, and against such conditions, many other drugs too will be described in the following book, some having a capacity similar to the phoenicine, others even more active. But against rheumatic affections this is the best drug of all, and it has often accomplished something greater than hope. When once a thigh suppurated near the groin, the inflammation throughout the whole of it being unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors would flow out toward the groin by way of the ulcer that had formed; and this having taken place over a longer time, the flux that had settled into the thigh was emptied out, but a certain fistulous condition arose under the skin along the whole thigh, so that I wished to cut it open near the knee-cap in order that there might be an outflow for the ichors on either side...

...having taken in addition vinegar; for that one is useful on every occasion, whereas the white one made with pepper is useful for burns that have been stripped of skin when they are being brought to a scar, but before that it is useless by itself, though when dissolved in myrtle oil it is useful, yet not with equal strength to the drugs that properly suit burns. Heras says it also suits those who have been bitten; but here too there is need of a distinction: for on hard and hard-to-concoct [bites] the drug is too weak, but on the more moderate ones it is sufficient, and especially in old men and children and women and, to say it in sum, the soft-fleshed. The drug is also useful for pimples, as Heras too wrote this truthfully; but about eruptions he pronounced without distinction, for of these also it treats those that are moderately somewhat hard, whereas those...

...but the measure is not equal to the Roman; for different people use different sextarius-measures. Among the Romans at any rate the sextarius holds one pound and a half and a sixth, so that the total ounces are 20, which they generally measure with horns incised on the outside with certain circular lines. Some, however, have falsely supposed the Roman sextarius to hold eighteen metric ounces. It seems, then, that Heras too, when he writes 'cotyle', signifies the half of the sextarius; but whether they mean the 9 ounces from the pound-horn or the ten, this is unclear. And whether the drug is also suitable for those bitten by mad dogs, whether swallowed or applied externally, cannot be known from reasoning; for it has been shown by us that such drugs have their activity by the whole peculiarity of their substance...

...concerning nourishment, that the bad and the not-bad are said as in relation to something, and clearly also the harmful and the beneficial. For in another sense you would say that the Attalic plaster is better than this plaster, in that it is more widely useful. Indeed Asclepiades himself, writing next after the one now described that very plaster made with white pepper, does not name it Attalic but Pamphilion, being ignorant, as I think, of the first discoverer of it, and having added the name of the one who used it and gave it to him. Its promise, then, he wrote word for word thus: 'Another, called Pamphilion, a well-contrived drug; it is effective for old and hard-to-heal [sores], carbuncles, epinyctides, scurfy affections of the scalp, mangy conditions; it glues together sinuses; it is effective for abscesses, condylomata'; and the drug is nearly more widely useful. He says it is composed of white lead...

...let each of these be exactly [so], for the sake of contributing something to the whiteness of the drug. About the white lead too it has been said before, and about the oil and the manner of the boiling and the surrounding air and the fire, how each of them might contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the other cases, so also in these, one who knows the capacities of water and of vinegar and of sea-water and of the whitest wine must mix in the composition what is most useful for the condition being treated. For in the case of ulcers with raised banks, whose lips are thick and hard and in need of much thinning, the [drugs] levigated with vinegar and sea-water are more useful than those with water; but in those in which the fluid carried in the ulcers is acrid and biting, one should rather levigate in water...

...each of the metallic [substances], just as again rather in wine in those cases where the fluid flowing onto the ulcers appears abundant. Each, then, of these which I mentioned, levigated for several days in each of the fluids mentioned, I put each time into all the drugs made with white lead and litharge, and I found them all cicatrising most finely; and I gave certain written recipes to friends who asked for such drugs, by whom too, when brought to the test, they appeared to preserve their promise. When, then, the litharge has been boiled beforehand, as has been said, with the white lead, and the drug has come near to a non-staining consistency, one must add larch resin or terebinth resin together with white wax, and when these have been well united, add in the metallic substances having the following proportion: of the litharge and the white lead, as usual, a pound of each, with two pounds of oil let it be boiled repeatedly...

...but if some scirrhous residue of its inflammation should remain, to apply one of the things that dry sufficiently. Since, then, something seemed to be lacking to the drug made with the root of dracontium, which I had used first (which has all else the same as the Egyptian drug called Isis, but has in addition the root of dracontium), next after this, having used the one called Athena, from that I passed on thereafter to the cicatrising agents. In another case, smearing on the exposed parts of the wound the trochisk dissolved in boiled-down must, I applied externally the euphorbium, having mixed it with wax and resin in such an amount as to make it at once plaster-like and to preserve the capacity of the euphorbium. How, looking to these aims, one might compound the drug, I shall say next; for indeed I also made another drug with vinegar...

...just as with the resin and the pitch; for this reason I mix with the cerate resin or pitch or a portion of each. It is clear, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil must no longer be put in equal to them; for the wax requires much of the fat for moistness, whereas of the resins the dry ones need altogether little, and the moist ones even want to take in some dry substance to reach a plaster-like consistency. Among the waxes, then, there is no great difference in moistness and dryness; but with the resins conversely, as also with pitch, the difference between the dry and the moist is very great. The driest of the resins is the one some call fried, others colophonian; second is the one from the pottery-kilns, unpurified and unfried; but if someone purify it...

...for me with the operation, some mixing in the same thing, of those inexperienced in the anatomy of all the muscles, flay off the underlying membranes, not knowing that these may be stitched together with the muscles without danger, but most dangerously the tendons that have been flattened out like them. But however much they themselves be flattened, nonetheless they are still thicker than the membranes and harder. You will see tendons sufficiently thin also in all the muscles at the epigastrium except the two straight ones, upon which the membranous aponeuroses of the oblique ones are laid; but no other tendon besides those mentioned is flattened in membranous fashion, for all those that are flattened preserve a sufficient thickness so as to escape no one. Yet the sympathy of the parts lying above, as far as the very origin of the nerves, [belongs] no less to the muscles at the end of the thigh and to those entering the elbow of the forearm and to those...

...you have seen me do throughout, not with this alone but also with the ammoniac incense. There is also the drug written after this by the Tarentine, of the same promise, according to this proportion: of chalcitis 25 drachms, of cadmia 12 drachms; having levigated them separately and mixed them, pour on undiluted wine, having boiled it, so that they be kneaded in due proportion; then levigate until it has dried, and having melted 50 drachms of wax, 30 drachms of terebinth resin, 8 cotylae of myrtle oil, mix with the cerate 20 drachms of the dry ingredients. And this drug has none of the emollient agents; yet in its mixing with the cerate, one trained rationally in the methods I have set out would appropriately work out the fitting quantity of the mixture for each of the ulcers. And rightly too the undiluted wine, that is, that with which sea-water has not been mixed...

...the meltable [ingredients], having let them cool somewhat, sprinkle onto these the dry ones, stirring carefully; and one must have, triturated with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium, opopanax, and into these what is in the dish is put and triturated so that lumps of wax do not form; and when it is in good order, take it up into a wooden box, having first smeared it with iris oil. On the third kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, about which Asclepiades wrote word for word as follows: 'For ulcers that do not come together at all, or that come together but break down again, either the flesh being corrupted or the underlying bones also being corrupted, one must use the following preparations. For chironian and hard-to-heal [ulcers], a well-contrived drug: of flake of copper, of scraped verdigris, 1 ounce each; of wax half a pound; of larch resin 1 ounce and a half. [Pour] the meltables over the dry ones, and having taken it up use it, kneading carefully and laying on a small flat piece over...'

...the metallic substances with vinegar, and after these adding in the dry ingredients and levigating again; then, when these have a mud-like consistency, mixing in the meltables as has been said before. Another: of asphalt and terebinth resin and Bruttian pitch, 1 pound each; of oil 24 drachms; of litharge and white lead and manna and verdigris and flake and opopanax, of each an amount equal to the twenty-four drachms of oil; of ladanum two ounces, which is 16 drachms; and two cotylae of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another: of chrysocolla and flake and stomoma, 4 drachms each; of verdigris and chalcanthum, the half of each, that is 2 drachms each; of wax 25 drachms, that is 3 ounces and one drachm; of terebinth resin 2 ounces, that is 16 drachms. Melt the wax with the terebinth...

...it checks haemorrhoids and works supremely well in affections about the bladder. It contains: of frankincense 4 drachms, of myrrh 4 drachms, of saffron 4 drachms, of Illyrian iris 4 drachms, of bdellium 4 drachms, of flake 12 drachms, of chalcanthum 4 drachms, of fissile alum 4 drachms, of round [alum] 4 drachms, of ammoniac incense 4 drachms, of misy 4 drachms, of rinds of sweet pomegranate 4 drachms, of aristolochia, of unripe oak-gall, 8 drachms each (otherwise 16), of chalcitis 4 drachms, of ammoniac incense 4 drachms, of oak mistletoe 8 drachms, of opopanax 8 drachms, of scraped verdigris 8 drachms, of acacia 8 drachms, of rose blossom 8 drachms, of terebinth 1 mina (others, 50 drachms), of poppy juice 6 drachms, of wax 2 minae (others, 4 drachms), of calf's suet, treated, 1 mina (others, 150), of common vinegar 2 cotylae, of wine [enough] for the dry ingredients. These...

Of verdigris of copper and of Indian aloe, of burnt copper and of good diphryges, sixteen and a half from each ingredient; twenty drachms of galbanum and 4; of manna of frankincense an equal amount, twice 12; of ammoniac twice 5 and twice 20; sixteen drachms of Attic propolis; of long aristolochia twice 10 drachms; twice 6 drachms of flake of Cyprian copper, and of the driest gentian root an equal amount. To all these add in of dittany herb, dry, bearing flower, 20 holkai. Having put litharge, levigated, with oil into a new wide-mouthed earthenware dish, boil over a light and soft fire, stirring with a spatula, until it gets the thickness of Attic honey; and having added in again an equal amount of the flake, boil more fiercely; then when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, making the drug non-staining and set; add the wax and the...

...of iris; and instead of the molybdaena put in two parts of litharge, and of the rest one part each. A dry septic [drug] of Lecanius Areius: of arsenic 1 pound, of quicklime 2 drachms; triturate in water for 30 days, changing the water twice a day, in the sun; then, having dried it out, use. A sitz-bath for haemorrhoids, that of Phanias: of chalcanthum, of fissile alum, of chalcitis, of raw misy, of sandarach, 4 drachms each; have them all finely levigated. At the time of use, put old pickled urine of a single man, in measure 2 sextarii, into an earthenware basin, and of the drug 12 drachms; pour in more of the urine so that the two sextarii are always maintained. Use this, sitting in it, for 7 days, for in these it is effective; and when it has become glutinous, smear the anus with the sediment. A dry [drug] that cicatrises flesh, non-biting, according to Harpocras: of sandarach, of chrysocolla, of arsenic, an equal amount of each...

...of wax, having neither of these, but with the ammoniac incense alone put in, will make the drug parched; but for plaster-making (for it is no worse to name it so) both the wax and the resin are useful; for the softening and the dispersing belong to the drug through the ammoniac alone, which holds the first place among the emollients and is a rival also among the discutients. And having recalled what was said in the 5th [book] of the Capacity of Simple Drugs, as to what sort of mixture such drugs must have, you will no longer need any newer instruction. For the first capacities active in drugs are in heat and cold and moisture and dryness; second are the emollient and discutient and repellent and attractive and concoctive and detergent and septic, just as also...

...of all carefully; again drip off a little; when you see it well-coloured and well-blended, take the pot at once from the fire and add galbanum previously softened. If the drug be much too hard, add oil to it for a good blending. Having thus strained it into another vessel, knead it cold with the hands, and so store it away. I shall set down another, of the same kind as the one before it; it is effective for the affections I mentioned earlier; this one cicatrises better than all drugs ulcers hard-to-heal and callous and chronic; the eruptions arising on the face this one cures without any harmful biting; fissures and hardnesses of the seat, the knotty ones, and calluses it casts off. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge (a mina is a pound and a third part of a pound), of good Pontic wax half a mina, of good scraped verdigris a fourth part of a mina...

...scrofulous swellings, reducing every oedema, and healing the watery conditions of the liver and spleen, drawing copious excretions of urine; it also releases long-standing sciaticas. Using this, Ulpianus, a well-gifted young man, helped very many. It contains one pound of Pontic wax, one of fried [resin] and one of pine resin, of fresh quicklime 1 ounce, of fissile alum 1 ounce, and equal to one of these of Pontic arsenic. Having poured on these a little fragrant vinegar, levigate them sufficiently in a larger mortar; having added a little oil to the wax and resin, melting it over a fire of fierce flame, and mixing all carefully, and making malagmata of a non-staining thickness, keep it stored away, using it where needed with a fresh compress. The Most Excellent, the father of the drug, said also that for deliverance from long diseases...

...which also heal the small inflammations. Of the compound emollients, some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first rank; some not much stronger than these, in the second; and some in the 3rd; others besides these in the 4th. One ought to use them, as has been said before, against slight hardnesses and soft bodies, those of the first rank; against bodies and affections stronger than these, those of the second, as likewise those of the third and the fourth proportionately. They also set down separately those under each of these. Menecrates did this because it often happens that errors are made in the written recipes not only by those who do so unwillingly but also, through envy, by some who do so willingly, making the letter o into th by drawing another transverse line through the middle of the round stroke, and the letter iota [into something else] by the addition of another similar transverse line; just as also when one stroke has been scraped off from the letter gamma, and from rho, the form of the iota is left behind. In the same way, from many letters, by addition in some, by combination in others, by removal in others, the alteration of the characters that signify them comes about. Yet Menecrates accomplished nothing more for the time to come, since those copying out his book did not write the names of the numbers in full letters but by the characters that signify them.
